newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary sorry Vranitzky goes despite soured ties.
newsitem.headline: Hungary sorry Vranitzky goes despite soured ties.

text.p: Hungarian commentators said on Monday they regretted Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's resignation but said his special relationship with Hungary had soured over European Union membership.

"I regret that Chancellor Vranitsky has resigned because he had very friendly feelings towards Hungary," Hungarian Foreign Minister Laszlo Kovacs said at the weekend. "His personal support for Hungary will be missed."

Vranitzky's resignation confounded political commentators in Austria who believed he was in for the long haul after surviving a leadership crisis in October following disastrous European Parliament elections.
However, Hungarian commentators suggested he had chosen the right time to bow out.

"The moment is right -- after 11 years he had become tired," said the daily Nepszabadsag, adding that his replacement, current finance minister Viktor Klima, could reinvigorate the Chancellor's post. @
"While, at 59, Vranitsky cannot be called old, his political post is being taken over by a man at the peak of his career," Nepszabadsag said.

Vranitzky received the most plaudits from Hungarian commentators for his role in the mid-1980s as an advocate of a flexible attitude to the most liberal of the Soviet Union's communist allies at a time when the Cold War was at its height.
"Vranitzky understood more what was going on in Hungary," Laszlo Valki, head of international law at Budapest's Lorand Eotvos University, told Reuters.
"He knew the policy of detente had much more to contribute to reform than the opposite policy which was pursued by others."

Valki added that while Germany became a more important ally in the months leading up to the fall of communism, Austria under Vranitzky remained a whole-hearted supporter of Hungary's European integration right up to Vienna's accession to the EU at the beginning of 1995.
The daily Magyar Hirlap saw that moment as signalling a cooling of Vranitzky's enthusiasm for Hungary's aspirations.
"Since Austria became a member of the EU...Vranitsky has shuffled back from promises to help Hungary and instead identified himself with the concerns of Burgenland," it said.

Burgenland, a rich agricultural area bordering Hungary, has lobbied against Hungary's early EU accession which it sees as undermining its competitiveness, especially in the labour market where Hungarian wages are a fraction of those in Austria.
"Vranitzky realised that if Hungary became a member of the community the price of the labour force would be an important matter," Valki said.
"The relative advantage which a foreign investor can get in Hungary is higher than in Austria and it is certainly a matter of competition between the two countries," he said.
The Magyar Hirlap said that Klima will just as cool on the issue.
"It is likely that Vranitzky's successor Klima will share the same careful reticence," it said.
However the Nepszabadsag added that while Austria's views on EU expansion were important they should not prove decisive. @
"It certainly matters whether torpedoes based on jealousy are sent from Burgenland to Brussels," it said. "But Austria will not be in a decisive position to influence (Hungary's EU entry)."
